Question: Let \(p(x) = x^3 + ax^2 + bx + c,\) where \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c\) are complex numbers. Suppose that \[ \begin{gathered} p(2009 + 9002\pi i) \\ = p(2009) \\ = p(9002) = 0. \end{gathered} \] What is the number of nonreal zeros of \(x^{12} + ax^8 + bx^4 + c?\)
Solution:
The exponents \(12,8,4\) suggest viewing the expression as \(p(x^4)\). This lets us use the known zeros without finding \(a,b,c\).

Let \(\alpha=2009+9002\pi i\). The three prescribed zeros of the monic cubic \(p\) are distinct, so the factor theorem gives
\[
p(t)=(t-2009)(t-9002)(t-\alpha).
\]
Consequently,
\[
p(x^4)=(x^4-2009)(x^4-9002)(x^4-\alpha).
\]
Every zero must therefore satisfy exactly one of the three fourth-power equations.

For a positive real number \(t\), put \(s=\sqrt[4]{t}>0\). The factorization
\[
x^4-t=(x-s)(x+s)(x-is)(x+is)
\]
shows that there are four distinct zeros, exactly two of which are nonreal. Thus \(t=2009\) and \(t=9002\) contribute two nonreal zeros each.

For \(x^4=\alpha\), the fundamental theorem of algebra guarantees a complex zero \(z\) of \(x^4-\alpha\). Since \(\alpha\ne0\), we have \(z\ne0\). The numbers
\[
z,\quad -z,\quad iz,\quad -iz
\]
are four distinct fourth roots of \(\alpha\). A polynomial of degree four has at most four distinct zeros, so this list is complete. None is real, because a real number's fourth power is real, whereas \(\alpha\) is nonreal.

The three groups are disjoint because a number has only one fourth power. Hence the number of nonreal zeros is
\[
2+2+4=\boxed{8},
\]
choice C.
